title: Quantitative Imaging of Chromatin Inheritance in Drosophila Germinal Stem Cells
author: Ranjan, Chen

steps.title: Generate dual‑color histone transgenes
steps.instruction: Use standard P‑element transformation to create UASp‑FRT‑Histone‑EGFP‑PolyA‑FRT‑Histone‑mCherry and the tag‑swapped version UASp‑FRT‑Histone‑mCherry‑PolyA‑FRT‑Histone‑EGFP; confirm construct integrity and integrate into the fly genome.

substeps.instruction: Construct plasmids with the dual‑color cassette.
Inject plasmids into w1118 embryos for P‑element mediated integration.

steps.title: Validate transgene copy number
steps.instruction: Genotype the resulting flies, map the chromosomal insertion site, and retain only lines that carry a single copy of the transgene for downstream experiments.

steps.title: Obtain cell‑type driver lines
steps.instruction: Acquire or generate a germ‑cell specific driver such as nanos‑GAL4 to express the dual‑color histone transgene in GSCs and early germ cells.

steps.title: Obtain hs‑FLP line
steps.instruction: Acquire a fly line carrying the heat‑shock promoter driven Flippase (hs‑FLP) transgene; Flippase will mediate FRT recombination after heat shock (37 °C, 90 min).

steps.title: Obtain α‑tubulin fluorescent line
steps.instruction: Acquire a transgenic fly line expressing a fluorescence‑tagged α‑tubulin (e.g., UASp‑tubulin‑GFP).

steps.title: Create balanced experimental stocks
steps.instruction: Generate balanced or homozygous stocks for (i) the dual‑color histone line, (ii) hs‑FLP; nanos‑GAL4, and (iii) nanos‑GAL4; UASp‑tubulin‑GFP; screen out balancer chromosomes in experimental flies because balancers may affect phenotype.

steps.title: Prepare live imaging medium
steps.instruction: Mix 8.5 mL Schneider’s Drosophila medium, 1.5 mL fetal bovine serum (15 % final), 6 µL penicillin/streptomycin (0.6×), adjust pH to ~7.0; just before use add insulin to a final concentration of 200 µg/mL (25 µL of 200 µg/mL stock) to make ~10 mL total. Aliquot medium without insulin and store at 4 °C for up to 5–6 months; aliquot insulin separately and store at –20 °C for up to 1 year; combine immediately before sample preparation.

steps.title: Induce tag switch by heat shock
steps.instruction: Subject flies carrying hs‑FLP to 37 °C for 90 min to activate Flippase, which recombines the upstream FRT‑flanked tag and switches expression from the first fluorescent tag (old histone) to the second (new histone). Allow the flies to recover for the duration indicated in the schematic (Figure 1C) before imaging.

steps.title: Live‑cell imaging of testes
steps.instruction: Dissect Drosophila testes, place them in the prepared live imaging medium, and acquire high‑resolution or super‑resolution Z‑stack images of GSCs, GBs, and SGs using a suitable microscope; ensure the entire nucleus is captured in each stack.

steps.title: Voxel‑based fluorescence quantification
steps.instruction: For each Z‑plane, measure the gray value of each voxel in the old‑histone (EGFP) and new‑histone (mCherry) channels, subtract the background gray value (Bs) from the signal (Rs) to obtain normalized voxel intensity (Rs‑Bs). Sum normalized intensities across all n stacks to get total fluorescence Fs = Σ(Rs‑Bs). Compute the GSC/GB ratio for each channel as Fs_GSC / Fs_GB; repeat the same calculation for SG1/SG2 pairs as controls.

substeps.instruction: Measure background intensity for each channel.
Subtract background from signal for each voxel.
Sum normalized voxel intensities across all Z‑stacks.
Calculate GSC/GB and SG1/SG2 ratios for old and new histone channels.

steps.title: Statistical analysis of histone inheritance
steps.instruction: Using the ratios from the previous step, calculate the old‑histone GSC‑to‑GB ratio, the new‑histone GSC‑to‑GB ratio, and the corresponding SG control ratios. Plot dot plots for each dataset, determine mean and standard error of the mean (SEM), and perform statistical tests. Define asymmetric inheritance when the GSC mean > (control SG mean + 1 × STD); define symmetric inheritance when the GSC mean < (control SG mean + 1 × STD).

steps.title: Assess chromatin condensation
steps.instruction: Select 15–25 GSCs and SGs; for each cell compute the compaction factor as the area occupied by the new‑histone‑enriched region divided by the area of the old‑histone‑enriched region. Generate dot plots, calculate mean, SEM, and statistical significance. Define differential condensation if GSC mean > (control SG mean + 1 × STD); define equal condensation if GSC mean < (control SG mean + 1 × STD).

steps.title: Measure nucleosome density
steps.instruction: Use 10–15 GSC‑GB pairs and 10–15 SG1‑SG2 pairs; calculate nucleosome density from the voxel fluorescence data (total fluorescence per unit volume). Plot dot plots, compute mean, SEM, and statistical significance. Define asymmetric nucleosome density when the GSC‑GB mean > (control SG mean + 1 × STD); define symmetric density when the GSC‑GB mean < (control SG mean + 1 × STD).

description: The protocol described here provides details on studying ACD of stem cells, epigenetic inheritance and cell fates. Stem cells are unique cell types that can undergo asymmetric cell division (ACD) to produce two distinct daughter cells. Studies have shown that extrinsic cues and intrinsic factors can regulate ACD. Previously, our studies have revealed that the preexisting (old) and newly synthesized (new) histones segregate asymmetrically during ACD of Drosophila male germline stem cells (GSCs). Importantly, the old histone is predominantly inherited by the stem daughter cell and the new histone is enriched in the differentiating daughter cells. This asymmetric histone inheritance is critical for GSC maintenance and differentiation. Recently, we have identified several unique chromatin features of Drosophila male GSCs during ACD, which regulate distinct cell fates and differential cell cycle progression in the resulting daughter cells, including differential sister-chromatid condensation in mitosis, which results in asymmetric chromatin accessibility to replication initiation factors and asynchronous cell cycle progression in the daughter cells. In addition, we have discovered that sister chromatids in GSCs have asymmetric nucleosome density, with the old histone-enriched sister chromatids having higher nucleosome density compared to the new histone-enriched sister chromatids. Here we detailed about developing genetic tools, in vivo live imaging and quantification methods to study ACD of stem cells. In summary, we propose that asymmetric nucleosome density could be used as a stem cell marker to distinguish stem cells at single-cell resolution, which could be widely appliable to many other systems including other stem cell lineages and asymmetrically dividing cells during development of multicellular organisms. These procedures will establish a new method for studying the ACD of stem cells and provide an imaging-based approach to study epigenome in the context of cell
